pages.text: $(li)You need: Pattern Terminal (create patterns), ME Interfaces (adjacent to machines), Molecular Assemblers, and a Crafting CPU.

$(li)Double-check patterns use correct ingot types (e.g., not Tinkers’ Antique variants) to avoid failures.$(li)For NBT-sensitive items (e.g., Rock Crystals), encode patterns with NBT-free blanks and let the crafter apply NBT.
$(li)A controller face carries 32 channels over dense cable; a network without a controller (energy acceptor only) gets just 8. Spread channels around the base with P2P tunnels or subnets.

$(li)AE2 autocrafters only craft full batches—if ingredients for even one full batch are missing, crafting is blocked.$(li)When multiple recipes share ingredients, the autocrafter gathers everything needed, then splits shared ingredients equally (rounded down) across consumers.

$(li)Use up to 6 Molecular Assemblers per Interface, and split crafting chains across separate columns (one chain per column) to maximize parallelization.$(li)Crafting card + export bus setups have a reputation for lag, though experienced players say it’s overblown.

$(l)Passive crafting$()$(li)Use Import Interfaces with partitioned cells to limit passive crafting to only what’s needed.$(li)Focus passives on high-use items: Alloys, seeds, chickens, Blood Magic slates, Thaumcraft Vis/Essentia.

$(li)Do $(o)not$() confuse batching (manual prep) with autocrafting—AE2 doesn’t do batching automatically.$(li)Use Export Buses with Fuzzy Cards for complex-NBT items to ensure correct extraction from AE networks
$(l)Avoid the Lazy AE2 Mass Assembler for 3×3 recipes$()—patterns may vanish unexpectedly; use standard AE2 autocrafters instead for reliability.
$(l)Route crafted patterns directly into the Lazy AE2 Mass Assembler$() using a high-priority storage bus to auto-fill it from your AE system.
